title: TreeWalker: Partial Evaluation for Grouped Tree-Ensemble Inference
claim: Standard inference re-evaluates shared inputs for every row; ours evaluates constant parts once and partitions rows only at varying splits.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, same tree; per-edge multiplicity counts vs bitmask flow
description: Two side-by-side panels share the same small decision tree and the same 4-row input table. Rows r0-r3 have constant x1=2, shaded grey, and varying x5=[2,4,7,9], shaded salmon. Panel (a), Standard inference, shows the tree with a dark navy root (x1≤3), an orange child (x5≤5) and green leaves (0.1, 0.2, 0.3). Edges carry repeat counts (×4, ×2, ×2), and the footer reads x1 evaluated 4×, x5 evaluated 4×. Panel (b), TreeWalker, uses the same tree. It adds a 1111 active-row bitmask above the root, a curved arrow labelled constant walk, and a split into 1100 and 0011 masks at the varying node. The footer reads x1 evaluated 1×, x5 partitioned 1×. The eye goes first to the bold panel titles, then to the colored tree nodes and the contrast between the repeat counts and the masks.
caption: Worked example: a 4-row group with shared x1=2 and varying x5=[2, 4, 7, 9]. (a) Standard inference evaluates x1 ≤3 four times and x5 ≤5 four times. (b) TreeWalker evaluates the constant split once, carries the active-row mask [1111], and partitions it at the varying split into [1100] and [0011] before leaf accumulation.
abstract: Many prediction tasks evaluate a trained tree ensemble on groups of rows that share feature values: discrete-time survival models expand each patient into $G$ time steps, click-through-rate models score every item in a search session, and scenario analyses vary a few inputs while holding the rest fixed. Standard inference treats each row independently and ignores this input-side correlation. We present TreeWalker, which instantiates partial evaluation for grouped tree-ensemble inference: constant features are static, varying features dynamic. TreeWalker walks each tree once per group, partitions a row bitmask at varying splits, and skips empty subtrees via an unsplit shortcut. It reads standard LightGBM and XGBoost models; training is unchanged. We prove a structural work decomposition: per-tree work splits into the constant-projected subtree size $|T_c|$, $G$ leaf writes, and a predicate-mask provisioning cost $Q$. For the trace evaluator, per-row work approaches $(d_v+1)/(d+1)$ as $G \to \infty$, giving asymptotic speedup $1/(1-\barÏ_G)$. On Intel, TreeWalker is ${\sim}3\times$ faster than a row-independent traversal at the reference model size ($T{=}500$, $L{=}8$; $G{=}16$ for SUPPORT/FLCHAIN and empirical groups for Expedia) and $7.7$--$9.1\times$ faster at $G{=}128$ on the survival datasets; on Arm, $2.5$--$2.9\times$ and $5.5$--$6.0\times$. On a scenario-analysis benchmark it is faster in all $16$ configurations on both machines. For f64 models, outputs match treelite GTIL up to tree-ordering roundoff; for f32 models, TreeWalker's f64 leaf accumulation is closer than native f32 to an exactly rounded reference on every audited row.
